articles.title_orig: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.title_zh: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.content_orig:
The brutal business of selling mirrors is not for the faint-hearted. The challenge is category differentiation, given that a mirror has one simple task—reflection. One of Greg Jackson’s first jobs was working for a mirror manufacturer which, at best, broke even or made a small profit. And then he had an idea.
“We started making mirrors that had really wide frames,” the founder of Octopus Energy (the U.K.’s largest energy provider) told me. “And on a picture [on the internet], suddenly we had a mirror that looked different from everybody else’s. And they sold like hotcakes – and that transformed the business.”
Approaching a business from a different point of view is an essential ingredient in the hunt for innovation. Jackson’s essential insight when it came to mirrors was that, online, every product looked the same. That is what the customer saw. And he realized that if the customer saw something different (a mirror with a wide frame), they might buy it. Which they did.
Not seeing something that is obvious to an outsider is a firm’s “incumbency cost”— embedded in the regular behavior of doing the same thing tomorrow as you did yesterday. It is one of the most significant brakes on the ability to grow.
“I think the single biggest factor affecting Europe—and an issue the U.S. is not immune to—is incumbency,” he told me. “China and the Gulf are not held back by incumbent industries. Instead they are, at huge pace, delivering the new world. If I look at electric vehicles as an example, there’s not an incumbent car industry in China that’s struggling to manage the transition to an entirely new technology. But if I look at Europe, European governments and consumers want electric vehicles, but the European car companies have not yet been able to be competitive at building them.”
“If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need”
Chinese electric vehicle sales in Europe are growing rapidly. Chery has tripled sales in Europe in the past year, BYD has doubled, Geely is up a third, and SAIC is up 23%. Taking the four leading Chinese car makers together, their EV market share is now at 14.6%, up from 9.6%, according to the latest figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. In response to claims of state subsidized dumping by China, the European Union has applied duties of up to 35% on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Chinese cars are still over 20% cheaper to buy.
“Incumbents crowd out the innovators in many sectors and markets,” Jackson said. “It wasn’t the Post Office [the UK’s public mail service] that invented email. The music industry held back streaming and digital music for 10 to 20 years. What you need is routes to market for new technologies, and I think that can be a challenge in Europe because so many of the big industries essentially have a stranglehold on policy.
“Economists have said that nearly all productivity growth comes from new companies. If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need.”
Jackson said that Europe has a number of successful sectors that it can learn from—for example, the continent enjoys a vibrant and innovative fintech sector whereas in America “they take my card around the back of the bar because their terminals and processes are so dated.” Few people have seen a check in Europe in more than a decade.
Octopus grew out of the need for a new way to manage energy supply and demand. Jackson initially attempted to convince legacy businesses that they would be far more efficient with a fully overhauled technology platform but, after not progressing very far, decided that he could build a team that could modernize more quickly.
“The idea was that through technology, we would be able to provide lower costs because we’d be more operationally efficient,” he said. “We’d be more agile, so we can incorporate technologies like electric vehicles and solar panels and batteries directly into the energy system very efficiently. That would also help with cleaning up energy because you can use more renewables more cost-effectively if you’re more agile. We set out building that company in 2015, and nine years later, we became the biggest energy company in the UK, overtaking all the incumbents.
“We came from outside energy, we came from tech, and just like the people that built Uber didn’t come from personal transportation, and the people that built Airbnb didn’t come from hospitality, and the people that built Amazon didn’t own bookshops. What we were able to do is build an energy company not based around the assumptions of the industry, but using technology to meet the needs of customers.”
The brute force of market dynamics is pushing the world towards a different energy mix. In the European Union, wind and solar power produced more electricity than fossil fuels for the first time last year, according to Ember, the energy think tank.
“The technologies of electricity are improving exponentially, and the technologies of hydrocarbons are not,” Jackson said. “A car engine costs roughly the same now as it did 20 years ago. They’re not particularly more efficient. Meanwhile, an electric vehicle battery today costs 10 times less than it did 15 years ago. Solar panels cost 200 times less than they did 40 years ago. Wind turbines have come down two thirds in price over the last 20 years.”
Jackson was in China earlier in the year and said that electrification is continuing at pace, with battery swap stations, rather than recharging, reducing the amount of time drivers have to wait to between three and five minutes. “It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is. The drivers don’t care about the price of diesel.” Which might give Donald Trump pause for thought as he eyes both the American mid-term elections and the rising cost of fuel in the U.S.
Kamal Ahmed is the executive editorial director of Europe and the Middle East. Kamal is the author of Letter from London , Fortune Europe's weekly take on global business as seen from London. Previously, he was director of audio at The Telegraph and presenter of The Daily T podcast.

articles.title_orig: Beijing rejects spy claims involving Nvidia CEO amid rising US-China tech tensions
articles.title_zh: Beijing rejects spy claims involving Nvidia CEO amid rising US-China tech tensions
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.
after newsletter promotion
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

articles.title_orig: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.content_orig:
The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds.
The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.”
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.
“ This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said.
As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value.
Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them.
Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X .
Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement.
The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.
Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million . Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead.
Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .
David Ingram is a tech reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq futures tumble as Amazon, Intel results deepen AI spending woes
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq futures tumble as Amazon, Intel results deepen AI spending woes
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Google’s parent company tumbled more than 12% on Thursday, their worst day on record — a historic single-day decline bigger than any day during the Covid-19 pandemic or 2008 financial crisis.
The drop erased roughly half a trillion dollars in Alphabet’s ( GOOGL ) market value, the second-largest single-day wipeout in history, after Nvidia’s nearly-$600 billion slide in early 2025 .
Investors are increasingly scrutinizing Big Tech’s AI spending spree and how the technology is affecting their own businesses — and Alphabet is their latest target.
The company’s shares dropped sharply as investors fretted over slowing growth in Google’s search advertising business occurring alongside a continued ramp-up in spending on AI.
The world’s largest technology companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build data centers, in a race to try and be among the winners of the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street is getting more cautious, attempting to sort out which companies are spending rationally, how those outlays are impacting other parts of their business, and who will actually benefit from AI’s transformative impact on society.
Alphabet reported quarterly sales figures on Wednesday that missed analysts’ expectations. Investors were dismayed by the miss in sales figures, which reignited longstanding concerns about whether the company’s cash cow — Google’s search advertising business — will be able to withstand the pressure of consumers increasingly using Google’s own (and competitors’) AI chat bots in the place of traditional search.
The fear is that this displacement might happen “faster than Google can react to it and pivot their business,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management.
The company also disclosed a second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow, another metric causing concern among investors. Since going public in 2004, Google — which became Alphabet in 2015 — hadn’t posted a single quarter of negative free cash flow until this year. Strong free cash flow is one sign of a healthy company that can pay dividends, conduct share buybacks and reinvest in its business.
Alphabet recorded $51.4 billion in capital expenditures in the third quarter alone, compared to $91.4 billion for the entire year in 2025. As the company ramps up its spending on AI, including data center construction, it’s leaving less cash for the kind of immediate gratification investors love, like share buybacks and dividends.
In stark contrast to Alphabet’s negative free cash flow, Microsoft reported this week that it had $18.6 billion in free cash flow in the third quarter, even as it continues to spend billions on its AI buildout. Microsoft’s shares ended the day flat on Thursday while Alphabet shares dropped more than 12%.
“We are now getting to see who is spending rationally on AI and who is not,” said Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners.
It might seem odd that shares of one of Big Tech’s biggest companies aren’t soaring after Anthropic filed its highly anticipated initial public offering prospectus just days earlier. Anthropic is committing to spending a lot of money to rent compute power from tech companies like Alphabet.
But that future promise isn’t guaranteed, especially if the data center buildout doesn’t go to plan or if AI isn’t as profitable as expected. Alphabet is asking investors to believe in its vision for AI and the data center buildout, while also trying to monetize AI and show it can generate strong returns from the technology.
Growth in Big Tech companies’ cloud computing divisions is a sign that demand for AI continues to be robust. But the market is on edge about anything that could go wrong for the AI boom.
Big Tech companies like Alphabet are turning to debt and financial markets to raise more capital to help fuel their ambitions. While companies say they are trying to keep up with demand, the competition for funds from investors is rising.
“Everybody is trying to get through the door at the same time, and it gives people pause,” said Ted Mortonson, an investment strategist at Baird who focuses on the tech sector.
Wall Street is becoming more disconcerting about the data center buildout, and companies that are burning through free cash flow are getting punished.

articles.title_orig: Sandisk Reports Another Big Earnings Beat. Investors May Have Wanted More.
articles.title_zh: Sandisk Reports Another Big Earnings Beat. Investors May Have Wanted More.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
"Sky-high pricing continues to drive results, but it looks to be decelerating sequentially," the research firm wrote.
SanDisk's Q1 revenue soared 380% to $11.03 billion, beating analysts' expectations.
Morningstar lowered its fair value estimate for SNDK to $870 from $1,000, which implies a 35% drop.
SanDisk Corp. (SNDK) tumbled over 4% in premarket trading on Friday despite an upbeat quarterly report. However, Morningstar analysts flagged that memory price growth appears to be slowing sooner than expected, with a peak on the horizon and a downcycle thereafter.
"Sky-high pricing continues to drive results, but it looks to be decelerating sequentially," the research firm wrote in its investor note on Friday. "To us, this indicates a pricing peak is on the horizon, in line with our thesis. Pricing is decelerating earlier and more quickly than we expected, and we still expect a severe downcycle after the peak."
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
The research firm pushed back on management's argument that long-term agreements would sustain high pricing, saying customers could renegotiate contracts or walk away if market prices fall below agreed levels.
While acknowledging strong AI demand growth, Morningstar said memory producers will significantly expand capacity between 2027 and 2029 to eventually bring prices down.
On the analyst call, SanDisk's CEO said the company "started fiscal year 2027 with another quarter of strong performance, with robust and growing demand for our products driving outpaced growth in our data center business."
"We see evidence to our thesis in recent results and guidance, with pricing growth decelerating quickly and revenue becoming volume-led," it said, adding that further risks for U.S. producers stem from the growth of the memory industry in China.
Morningstar lowered its fair value estimate for SNDK to $870 from $1,000, implying a 35% drop from the stock's Thursday closing price. SanDisk shares have rallied over 460% year-to-date.
SanDisk's fiscal first-quarter revenue soared 380% to $11.03 billion, beating market expectations of $10.72 billion, according to FactSet data. Adjusted profit also came in higher than expected at $49.51 per share, up from $46.67 per share in the year-ago quarter.
For the fiscal second quarter, SanDisk forecast revenue of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion and adjusted earnings of $55 to $57 a share. Analysts had expected $12.31 billion and $53.60.
The company announced an 8-for-1 stock split, effective Nov. 19.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for SNDK shifted from 'extremely bullish' to 'neutral,' amid 'high' message volume. "$SNDK $200 billion company netting $8 billion per quarter with $9 billion cash flow is actually absurd. I don't care what the cyclical or bubble theory is… you cannot hold those earnings down for long," a trader wrote .

articles.title_orig: Amazon, Alphabet, SpaceX and Meta are all to blame for the new tech stock rout
articles.title_zh: Amazon, Alphabet, SpaceX and Meta are all to blame for the new tech stock rout
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Don't blame Intel's ( INTC ) weak guidance, tied to a prolonged memory chip supply shortage , for the fresh rout on tech stocks.
Blame the hyperscalers like Amazon ( AMZN ), Alphabet ( GOOGL ) and Meta ( META ) for not guiding Wall Street properly on how much they intended to spend this year and next on AI infrastructure. The bills are coming in much larger than expected, and Wall Street can't stomach it.
That's why you aren't seeing many heroes out there saying buy the dip right now. That's why Friday is shaping up to be another bloodbath for tech stocks.
Remember, it's cash flow that will be used to repay all the debt hyperscalers are poised to incur to support their robust AI infrastructure buildouts. The fact that cash flow is drying up because of a protracted period of spending is the bug causing the debt and stock markets to catch a cold.
Kudos to Amazon for at least not burying its free cash flow metric, the most important metric for tech at the moment, at the bottom of its earnings release. It made it no less tough to stomach, but at least it was easy to find quickly.
Amazon's free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a year-over-year increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment. This increase primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence, Amazon said.
This compares to a free cash flow inflow of $14.8 billion for the trailing twelve months ended Sept. 30 of last year.
"We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on his earnings call.
Amazon's stock is down 7% in pre-market trading today.
On Wednesday evening, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the quarter versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion.
Thursday saw more than $500 billion in market value wiped off Google.
Meta dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results last week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012. SpaceX ( SPCX ) burned about $9.9 billion in free cash flow in the quarter.
Both stocks have continued to sell off post earnings.
Hyperscaler free cash flow is likely to stay negative points out EvercoreISI strategist Julian Emanuel. The hyperscaler cohort of Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle ( ORCL ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) is now near a negative $200 billion expected over the next year Emanuel's research shows.
This is what the market is pricing in today. Painful, yes.
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title_orig: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.title_zh: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.content_orig:
Volkswagen is done keeping its Chinese software locked inside China. The automaker said its China Electronic Architecture (CEA), built with local electric vehicle maker Xpeng , will underpin next-generation models bound for South America and South Africa. That marks a sharp break from the brand's old "in China, for China" approach.
Now that same software stack is being lined up for Europe. A report summarized by Reuters says Volkswagen is studying whether the China Electronic Architecture could form the basis for future mass-market cars from its VW, Skoda, and Cupra brands in Europe, with the plan still under discussion inside the group.
As reported by Reuters , Volkswagen plans to integrate China-developed technology into South American product lineups starting in 2030 . Volkswagen Group China now uses the China Electronic Architecture in five locally produced all-electric Volkswagen brand models, including the Yuzhong 06 and Yuzhong 07.
Volkswagen Group China laid out the broader package, called VEGA, at a Technology Day event in Hefei. VEGA ties together the China Main Platform, the China Electronic Architecture, and China-developed software and driver-assistance systems into one scalable package for software-defined vehicles across multiple segments.
The China Main Platform targets A-segment battery-electric and plug-in-hybrid models. Volkswagen's stated goal is more than 373 miles of CLTC range and roughly 11 kWh per 62 miles in its most efficient version. Volkswagen says the China-built software could extend further still, with the Europe proposal covering roughly three quarters of the next-generation lineups for VW, Skoda, and Cupra .
Exports of China-developed vehicles are also starting to ramp up around 2026. China-built Volkswagens are already heading to markets such as Mexico and parts of Southeast and Central Asia, with more destinations planned afterward. That export push would run alongside the deeper platform integration planned for 2030.
The architecture trims the number of electronic control units by about 30 percent compared with Volkswagen's older setups. Volkswagen says that reduction is central to cutting development costs and complexity across its lineup.
It's a hardware play as much as a software one. Volkswagen intends to bring the same architecture to plug-in-hybrid and combustion models in China by 2027, which would widen its reach past the battery-electric vehicles where it currently lives and give future gas and hybrid products the same software backbone.
Looking further out, Volkswagen is targeting Level 4 automated driving by 2029, built on a third-generation version of the China Electronic Architecture paired with a Volkswagen-developed C7H control chip. That automated-driving target sits alongside the South America plan and the potential European rollout.
The strategy also threatens to sideline Rivian , Volkswagen's US software partner in a $5.8 billion investment central to CEO Oliver Blume's technology plans. A separate report from German outlet Manager Magazin said core brand chief Thomas Schäfer is weighing a proposal to use China-developed software as the basis for future Volkswagen, Skoda, and Cupra models, which would leave Rivian focused on other group brands even if the joint venture itself stays in place.

articles.title_orig: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.title_zh: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent the week punishing Big Tech's biggest AI spenders . Amazon ( AMZN ) just posted the deepest cash burn in its history.
Amazon's free cash flow — the cash left after paying for data centers, warehouses, and equipment — was an outflow of more than $42 billion over the 12 months through September, according to its third quarter results released Thursday. That's nearly double the previous record of about $23 billion, set in 2022 after Amazon overbuilt its warehouse network. Three months earlier, the outflow was less than $8 billion.
One quarter did most of the damage. Amazon spent about $77 billion on property and equipment from July through September, more than double the $35 billion it spent a year earlier. Its operations brought in about $42 billion, leaving a gap of roughly $33 billion over three months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
So far, the spending is working.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) grew 39% to about $46 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon's operating margin of nearly 14% was its highest ever. CEO Andy Jassy said in the release that he projects AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) computing commitments alone amount to about a fifth of AWS's backlog as of June , according to Yahoo Finance calculations based on the AI lab's IPO filing.
Paying for it has meant borrowing. Amazon's long-term debt reached about $173 billion at the end of September, up from about $66 billion at the end of 2025, while its cash fell to about $56 billion from about $87 billion. Meta ( META ) took a different route this week with a nearly $100 billion stock sale .
Bond traders have noticed. The cost of insuring Amazon's debt against default for five years with credit default swaps has risen about 50% since early August, according to Bloomberg data. That price implies roughly a 7% chance of default over five years, up from about 5%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Amazon stock fell about 4% Thursday to its lowest close since July 30 as Alphabet's record drop weighed on Big Tech. It slid further after-hours as sales, earnings, and its profit outlook for the holiday quarter missed estimates.

articles.title_orig: French centrists' feuding increases odds of Le Pen-Melenchon runoff
articles.title_zh: French centrists' feuding increases odds of Le Pen-Melenchon runoff
articles.content_orig:
The protests in France have handed Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the country’s far Left, a boost in his presidential campaign.
Polling conducted after the Oct 17 protests shows that Mr Mélenchon has pulled ahead of Édouard Philippe, an ally of Emmanuel Macron, the French president, to become the biggest challenger to Marine Le Pen.
According to the survey, which was conducted for the newspaper Le Parisien, Mr Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, has gained two percentage points since civil unrest peaked in France last weekend, putting him at 17 per cent in the first round compared with an average of 14 per cent for Mr Philippe.
Ms Le Pen, the leader of the hard-Right National Rally, boasts a strong lead , with an average of 33 per cent.
For months, polls predicted that the voting booths would pit Ms Le Pen against Mr Philippe, the leader of the centre-right Horizons party.
But the events of Oct 17, when 550,000 people took part in nationwide protests that spiralled into chaos and looting, have upended the campaign on the Left.
Brice Teinturier, the deputy director general of the polling firm Ipsos, credited Mr Mélenchon’s full-throated support for the student revolt that kicked off last month.
“He has repeatedly emphasised the need to listen to the protesters; that is what has enabled him to rise to prominence,” Mr Teinturier told Le Parisien. “The real protesters have been forgotten by many, but not by him.”
The poll surveyed 1,500 people registered on the electoral lists between Oct 21 and 22.
French students began blockading schools last month to protest against teacher shortages and crumbling schools. Since then, they have been joined by trade unionists and the “yellow vest” movement from 2018, in a convergence of grievances that include the rising cost of living and the erosion of public services.
The protests have driven new momentum for the far Left, and diverted support from Ms Le Pen to her far-Right rival, Éric Zemmour.
Mr Philippe, who served as prime minister for three years under Mr Macron , is losing ground amid fierce anti-government and anti-Macron sentiment. In the best-case scenario, Mr Philippe is projected to secure 15 per cent of the vote in the first round of voting.
“The French believe the government has made poor decisions. Consequently, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, who are part of that government, are being heavily penalised. This trend is accelerating for them,” Mr Teinturier said.
Raphaël Glucksmann, the presidential candidate for the socialists, is also closing the gap with Mr Philippe, with an average of 13 per cent, and has the added advantage of presenting voters with new blood over the old guard.
While the riots were also expected to give Ms Le Pen a boost, the polling shows that they have instead strengthened support for Mr Zemmour, the leader of the ultra-Right-wing Reconquête party, which currently has the support of 4 per cent of voters.
“Marine Le Pen dominates the scene, but she is not capitalising on current events,” Mr Teinturier said.
“She is losing ground as voters are turning back to Zemmour.”
On Sunday, Ms Le Pen launched her presidential campaign in the city of Orleans in front of 8,500 supporters.
Students from the Union of Jewish Students of France infiltrated the rally and heckled Jordan Bardella, the party’s newly re-elected president, during his speech.
Mr Bardella was quick to denounce “this ultra-Left who doesn’t like democracy” and the audience started singing “La Marseillaise” as the protesters were removed.
In her hour-long speech, Ms Le Pen pledged to “restore the rule of law” by automatically and permanently deporting “foreign delinquents” and making rioters pay for damage “their whole life” if they have to.
Without mentioning Ukraine by name, she also said she wanted to make France “a nation of peace” and promised not to send young people to die in “wars that are not ours”.

articles.title_orig: German president confident of resolving trade disagreements with China
articles.title_zh: German president confident of resolving trade disagreements with China
articles.content_orig:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is confident Germany and China can resolve trade disagreements.
A recent agreement on limiting hybrid car exports to the European Union showed that even where things were difficult "there is a way to find solutions," Steinmeier said at the start of his meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing on Friday.
Steinmeier directly addressed the growing imbalance in bilateral trade relations. Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.
"We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.
When there were problems, Germany would work "to solve them together with you through dialogue," he said.
Steinmeier said China remained important as Germany's largest trading partner and praised the country's "breathtaking pace" in technological and economic development.
Li called Steinmeier a "long-time and good friend" of China.
Germany's president holds a largely ceremonial role but frequently speaks on foreign policy and international affairs.
Steinmeier concludes his nearly week-long visit to China on Friday and is also due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu bloc short of majority as Arab parties secure record seats
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu bloc short of majority as Arab parties secure record seats
articles.content_orig:
Final results from Israel's pivotal legislative election this week showed there was no clear winner, with both of the two main blocs well short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc finished on 53 seats, while the opposition camp, led by the centrist Yashar party of rival Gadi Eisenkot, ended on 48.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party remained the largest party, with 27 seats, while the Arab parties secured a record 19 seats between them.
The result means Israel is now set to face a lengthy and likely tricky period of negotiations as party leaders work to form a government. Failure to do so would see Israelis head back to the polls.
Netanyahu has accused Arab parties of "stealing" the election, calling on police and Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet to carry out a "thorough investigation into election fraud."
The Likud party also pushed claims that foreign funding had been used to influence voters in the election. The allegations focused on claims that the Ra'am party had received money from Qatar.
"The ‘Ra’am-gate’ scandal is an earthquake. The Israeli elections have been stolen," Likud said in a statement on Thursday.
Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas reportedly denied any wrongdoing and said he would welcome an investigation.
In a post on social media, Eisenkot said foreign interference was "unacceptable and extremely serious" and called on Shin Bet to investigate the allegations "fully and immediately, without bias."
Moving forward, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with leaders of the parties elected to the Knesset before assigning the task of trying to form a government to the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing sufficient support to do so.
Under Israeli law, that individual will have 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.
Should that fail, the president can give a second leader the chance to form a government, this time with a maximum deadline of 28 days. If this second round were also to fail, then the Knesset can request a third candidate be given a go. They would have 14 days to complete the task.
If all attempts fail, another election is called.

articles.title_orig: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has said that about $6.3bn in funds have been stolen in a “security incident” that looks to be the biggest crypto heist in history.
The world’s largest crypto exchange said on Thursday that it had suspended all deposits and withdrawals and that about $3bn in funds had been frozen following the apparent hacking.
Binance said an initial investigation suggested that a hacker had been able to make unauthorised transactions after gaining access to an engineer’s compromised laptop.
The company said it would cover all losses, adding that user funds were “safe”.
“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
The company added that it would share a “detailed” technical post-mortem once investigations were complete.
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder and largest shareholder, said earlier that the exchange appeared to have been hacked.
TRM, a blockchain intelligence firm, said in a report that it assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by North Korea’s hacking unit TraderTraitor, which investigators have linked to the Lazarus Group.
Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, described the attack as “unprecedented” and a “watershed”.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity. That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Redbord told Al Jazeera.
The price of Bitcoin, the world’s most popular cryptocurrency, fell about 5 percent following the heist, dropping below $77,000.
“Binance is one of the largest centralised exchanges, and so a blow to confidence in them risks shocking confidence to many retail investors, which could dampen prices of crypto assets,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Foley said the attack highlighted the risks of centralised exchanges and could spur more traders to use decentralised alternatives.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Foley said.
The Binance hacking dwarfs the previous record for a crypto theft, set in 2025 when North Korean state-backed Lazarus Group carried out a $1.5bn heist on Bybit.
Cybercriminals stole $2.87bn in crypto assets in nearly 150 hacking incidents in 2025, according to the 2026 Crypto Crime Report produced by TRM.
Binance, founded in China by Zhao in 2017, has about $155bn in assets under management, more than any other exchange, according to CoinMarketCap.

articles.title_orig: Global tech rout deepens as US earnings stoke AI spending fears
articles.title_zh: Global tech rout deepens as US earnings stoke AI spending fears
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Iain Withers and Ankur Banerjee
LONDON/SINGAPORE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Tech shares slumped on Friday and US bonds surged toward their biggest monthly gain in nearly three years, as investors scurried to safety due to worries that huge and rising AI spending may not deliver ‌sufficient returns.
Futures trading pointed to falls on Wall Street later in the session, including a more than 2% drop in the tech-heavy Nasdaq ‌100. That came alongside an out-of-hours plunge of 23% in Intel shares and a drop of 7% in Amazon as their results showed they burned through cash.
Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell 12.6% on ​Wall Street on Thursday and slid a little further after hours, to wipe out a stunning $500 billion in market value, as massive AI spending turned the company's cash flow negative.
European stocks opened down 0.2% on Friday, as the relative lack of big tech stocks helped limit losses. There were falls earlier in Asia led by chipmakers.
Investors are worried about the returns they can expect to make on the massive capital spending needed for the AI buildout and what effect it could have on consumers if ‌price hikes squeeze global demand for devices like smartphones ⁠and PCs. Anthropic's potentially record-breaking IPO could prove the next big test of sentiment.
"The next key milestone will be the Anthropic IPO, to see how that lands. If it's a poor listing, I think that could signal a bit of ⁠weakness going forward," said Jason Da Silva, co-chief investment officer at Arbuthnot Latham.
Nerves were also frayed by a potentially record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, which drove down bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency, bitcoin, hit a six-week low before cutting losses to trade 1.1% lower at $77,876.
"I suspect the negative price action still ​has ​some way to go," said Geoffrey Kendrick, head of digital assets research at Standard ​Chartered. "Only after assets are unfrozen and more detail of the ‌hack emerges will we find a new base."
In commodities, oil prices rose about 2% on Friday and were poised for a fourth monthly gain, as an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz waterway highlighted continuing supply risks from the US-Israeli war on Iran. [O/R]
The Bank of Japan left interest rates on hold, which was expected and did not trigger major currency or bond moves, although in a surprise development the central bank unveiled plans to sharply accelerate exchange-traded fund sales next year.
"While this may initially spook markets, I actually think this is a positive development since the BOJ feels confident ‌enough with the economy and market," said David Chao, global market strategist for Asia-Pacific at ​Invesco.
The central bank declared victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its price target and ​signalled vigilance against inflation risks, suggesting the next rate hike could ​come as soon as December.
Tech sector jitters have helped push a rush to bonds, further spurred by the Federal Reserve's ‌decision on Wednesday to keep US interest rates on hold, with ​no firm projection of when it might ​hike next.
Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields fell around 7 basis points on Friday to 4.92% and were on track for their largest one-month drop since December 2023. Yields fall when bond prices rise.
The risk-averse mood strengthened haven currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc, with the ​yen slightly higher at 157.30 per dollar and the ‌franc at 0.821 to the dollar and not far from a one-month high.
The euro inched up 0.1% to $1.1194 but was set for ​a drop of over 1% in October, its second straight monthly decline.
(Reporting by Iain Withers in London and Tom Westbrook and Ankur ​Banerjee in Singapore; Editing by Tom Hogue, Clarence Fernandez, Stephen Coates, William Maclean)

articles.title_orig: China seeks to strengthen cooperation with Iceland in Arctic affairs
articles.title_zh: China seeks to strengthen cooperation with Iceland in Arctic affairs
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, center left and Zhang Shengmin, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission second from right attend a ceremony in honor of fallen national heroes at the Monument to the People's Heroes to mark Martyrs' Day at Tiananmen Square in Beijing, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.
During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.
The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.
The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.
The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.
Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.

articles.title_orig: Prince Albert of Monaco’s cousin Antoine de Massy, 29, found dead as Ukrainian man is charged
articles.title_zh: Prince Albert of Monaco’s cousin Antoine de Massy, 29, found dead as Ukrainian man is charged
articles.content_orig:
Prince Albert of Monaco’s cousin has been found dead after leaving a nightclub — while a 42-year-old Ukrainian man has been charged in connection with the royal relative’s death.
Antoine De Massy’s body was discovered Sunday in a park along Boulevard du Larvotto, in Monaco’s upscale Larvotto district, after his family alerted authorities when they were unable to reach him.
De Massy, 29, was allegedly seen leaving a nightclub Sunday night, staggering and leaning on a man for support, according to Le Parisien .
According to an autopsy, de Massy likely died after “a fall from a height of 13 meters,” Monaco Prosecutor General Stéphane Thibault told Agence France-Presse Wednesday.
A Ukrainian national, who has lived in Monaco for 30 years, was arrested and charged Wednesday with involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist a person in danger.
The suspect, who has not been identified, denied the allegations during police questioning before appearing before an investigating judge, whom he refused to answer, Thibault said. He was subsequently remanded in custody.
The charges do not allege that de Massy was intentionally killed, and the suspect is presumed innocent.
Authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding de Massy’s death to establish “the precise sequence of events that led to [his] fall,” Thibault said.
A memorial has since appeared near the scene of his death, featuring flowers, candles, a Monaco flag and tennis balls in tribute to de Massy’s passion for the sport.
De Massy was the son of Baron Christian de Massy, Prince Albert’s first cousin, and Cécile Gelabale. His grandmother, Princess Antoinette, was the elder sister of Prince Rainier III and Prince Albert’s aunt.
The prince, 68, and his wife, Princess Charlène, 48, confirmed the family tragedy in a statement released by the Prince’s Palace on Monday.
“Their Serene Highnesses Prince Albert II and Princess Charlène were saddened to learn of the death of Antoine de Massy, aged 29, the grandson of Princess Antoinette, the elder sister of Prince Rainier III,” the statement read.
“A keen tennis player, he was part of a family history closely linked to the sport in the Principality. Their Highnesses share in the grief of his family and loved ones and offer them their sincere condolences at this painful time,” it added.
De Massy followed in the footsteps of his paternal grandfather, Alexandre-Athenase Noghes, an international tennis player, and had hoped to represent Monaco at the Olympics.
Prince Albert has faced his share of controversies over the years, including a paternity scandal involving two children born outside his marriage and allegations of cheating .
Albert has also faced scrutiny over leaked financial records from former palace accountant Claude Palmero, which detailed lavish spending, secret payments and alleged surveillance within the royal household.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s party claims election ‘stolen’ as results show him losing majority
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s party claims election ‘stolen’ as results show him losing majority
articles.content_orig:
Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority
Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel , supposedly funded by foreign money.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.
“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.
The prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.
On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online , which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.
Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power .
Final results released early on Friday local time showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and Eisenkot’s bloc taking 48 seats. Joint List and Ra’am won the remaining 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.
The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition from voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.
The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”
Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.
Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.
Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.
The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.
The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.
It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.
The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.
On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.
Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.
Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.
The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.
One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.
Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.
“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset.
Results released by election officials early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday.
Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!” it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was “aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government.”
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”
As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot , said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. “They are doing this because they lost,” he said.
Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: “I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel.”
Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.
Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab citizens of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population but are often viewed with suspicion because of their sympathies with other Palestinians.
Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before.
On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of “attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular.”
“Netanyahu is working to steal the election,” the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday.
The head of the Arab-led Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement.
President Isaac Herzog called it a “sensitive moment” and called for a full investigation. He warned that “we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy.”
The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with him.
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc’s candidate.
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.

articles.title_orig: US Lawmakers Condemn Lavrov’s G20 Visit as Russia Continues Attacks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: US Lawmakers Condemn Lavrov’s G20 Visit as Russia Continues Attacks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Atlanta on Friday, Oct. 30 for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting despite objections from US lawmakers and European allies. Moscow plans to challenge Western sanctions as Washington prepares new peace talks involving Ukraine and Russia.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in the US on Friday, Oct. 30, for a G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, despite calls from US lawmakers to bar him from the country while Moscow continues its war and deadly attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
Lavrov’s arrival, reported by Russia’s state-owned TASS news agency, comes days after Russian strikes killed civilians across Ukraine, including 14 people at a railway station in Dnipro.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The Kremlin’s top diplomat, under US sanctions since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, is expected to use the Oct. 30-31 gathering to criticize Western sanctions against Moscow, according to Russia’s Foreign Ministry.
Republican Rep. Don Bacon sharply condemned Lavrov’s visit, calling for the Russian foreign minister to be barred from entering the US while Moscow continues its deadly attacks on Ukrainian cities.
“Lavrov should not be allowed in the country. As long as Putin is waging war against Ukraine and bombing cities, Russian leaders should not be welcomed in any of these forums. They lead a pariah state,” Bacon wrote on X on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, also sharply criticized Trump’s approach to Moscow, demanding that Washington stop extending diplomatic legitimacy to Putin’s regime while Russian forces continue killing Ukrainian civilians.
“Donald Trump needs to wake up,” Shaheen said in an Oct. 8 CNN interview. “He needs to understand that courting favor with Vladimir Putin is not good for America.”
Shaheen, who joined 13 bipartisan senators in calling for Putin and other sanctioned Russian officials to be barred from G20 events on US soil, urged the administration to increase pressure on Moscow rather than reward it with international recognition.
In their letter to Trump , the senators questioned why Russia should receive diplomatic legitimacy while continuing its deadly attacks on Ukraine’s cities and civilian infrastructure.
The bipartisan criticism comes just days before the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, with the Trump administration facing questions over its approach to Moscow amid continued Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Lavrov would use his appearance to argue against economic sanctions and other trade restrictions, portraying them as instruments of pressure.
The Russian delegation also intends to promote Moscow’s vision of a multipolar international order.
The visit comes as Washington prepares new trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine, and Russia, expected in November in Abu Dhabi.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the G20 gathering, which will address major international disputes alongside energy security, trade and global supply chains.
The meeting also precedes the Dec. 14-15 G20 leaders’ summit at President Trump’s Doral resort in Miami, to which Putin has been invited. His attendance remains unconfirmed.
According to the State Department’s delegation list, Lavrov is attending alongside foreign ministers from major NATO and European countries, including Germany’s Johann Wadephul, France’s Jean-Noël Barrot, Poland’s Radosław Sikorski, Canada’s Anita Anand, and Turkey’s Hakan Fidan.
Other participants include EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Britain’s Ed Miliband, Australia’s Penny Wong, India’s Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, and Japan’s Toshimitsu Motegi.
China is represented by Executive Vice Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu rather than Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
Ukraine was not invited, although it had participated in previous G20 meetings as a guest. US officials said the decision reflected a policy of limiting invitations to formal members. South Africa was also excluded amid tensions with Washington.
Russia’s participation has unsettled some Western allies, who have questioned the invitation while Moscow intensifies its attacks on Ukraine.
The G20 meeting opens as Washington seeks renewed diplomatic engagement with Moscow, while Ukraine and its European partners continue pressing for stronger sanctions and security guarantees.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Officials at the Pentagon have in recent weeks asked several Nato countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia , ‌arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.
Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania , Latvia and Estonia , said the people, who spoke ​on condition of anonymity.
It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.
The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia – including sanctions relief – with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: “Private conversations among allies are just that, ​so we will not comment on these allegations.”
Among the comments that have drawn US officials’ attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.
Pentagon ⁠policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said.
None of the people, who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.
The US messages reflect a debate within Nato regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.
Some Western officials have argued that ⁠emphasising the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which ​they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others argue European governments must be transparent ​to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the Continent.
Russia has denied that it is pursuing ‌such a campaign.
One of the people familiar with the contacts said Colby ​told a Baltic official recently that there should be no “poking” directed at the Russians.
The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was “cornered like a rat” as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It ⁠was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian prime minister Kristen ⁠Michal referred to Putin as a “rat in a corner” ​in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon’s recent private messaging. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.”
In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.
The defence ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while Nato declined to comment.
One of the European officials said that the Pentagon’s advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic States have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing Nato’s mutual defence provisions.
Other Nato intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the ‌near future.
The Pentagon messages to Nato officials come ⁠at a fraught time for European security.
Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on Nato countries, Western intelligence officials have said.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle ‌Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.
At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration’s push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for ​the Kremlin’s continued economic isolation.
Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington’s force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in ​America’s troop presence on the Continent.
US officials have said European Nato members need to assume more responsibility for their own defence, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.
Meanwhile, an aid convoy started moving overnight towards ‌the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, carrying food and medical supplies among other items, the Russian newspaper ‌Izvestia said on Friday.
The move follows weeks of efforts to organise a relief operation for residents of the ​acutely deprived town, seized by Russian forces soon after Moscow’s February 2022 invasion of its smaller neighbour.
Ukraine human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, each wearing patches showing their nation’s flags, met by night ​in video images released by Russian state TV channel Vesti.
“Is everything all right?” Lantratova asked in Russian in the ⁠clip. “Yes, we were warmly welcomed,” Lubinets replied in Ukrainian.
The channel said the meeting ‌was ‌in ​Oleshky. A fleet of 25 buses with at least 750 seats stood ready to evacuate those seeking to leave, including pets, Lantratova ⁠said.
Russian newswires quoted Lantratova as ​saying Moscow and Kyiv were sticking to their ​agreements, while a ceasefire was holding to enable aid to the town. Both commissioners and ‌the US side had helped mediate the ​ceasefire.
Reporters from countries such as France, Italy, Russia, Ukraine and the United States are ⁠accompanying the convoy, according to Izvestia.
On Thursday, ⁠Russia and Ukraine ​said demining operations had been completed around Oleshky and the operation was ready to begin, to deliver aid to residents and let some leave.
Two people were killed in the demining effort in Oleshky, Lantratova said on Friday.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, Russia struck an industrial facility near Kremenchuk while hitting the capital, Kyiv and Kharkiv, the second biggest city, to cause fires, officials said on the Telegram messaging ‌app, after deadly strikes ⁠a day before.
Russia has struck military facilities in Ukraine, the Russian defence ministry said on Telegram on Friday.
It added that it hit energy infrastructure in ‌and around Kyiv, as well as in the Dnipropetrovsk region, port facilities in the Odesa region and cargo ​vessels it said were used by the military.
Russian authorities downed ​most of the more than 850 drones headed overnight towards Moscow, the capital’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanian said on Telegram. – Reuters

articles.title_orig: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
articles.title_zh: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
69 people have been confirmed dead but the toll may rise further, with at least 70 people reported missing
Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez and Castilla–La Mancha president Emiliano García-Page have just briefed the media on the latest on the train crash on Wednesday.
69 people have been confirmed dead, but the toll may rise further, with at least 70 people reported missing. Some may be among those yet to be identified, with emergency services having so far confirmed the identities of only 13 people. A further 31 body bags containing partial remains also await identification, making the process “very complex.”
Sánchez added that there may be up to 27 nationalities among the affected, with authorities working in close coordination with relevant embassies and consulates.
Out of 110 people hospitalised after the incident, 71 have been discharged, and 39 remain in hospitals.
The prime minister also acknowledged that the confidence in the country’s high-speed train, once a source of national pride , is “broken” as he pledged to work on restoring it in the future.
“The government’s job is not just to make the diagnosis, but to offer solutions so that a tragedy of this magnitude never happens again. And that’s what we’re doing,” he said.
I will bring you the key lines.
As we are still waiting for Puente’s press conference, we are getting more information about foreign victims of the crash.
A Czech citizen died in Wednesday’s train crash in Spain, the Czech foreign ministry has confirmed, according to the ČTK news agency.
Earlier today, Portugal also confirmed that its citizen was among the victims ( 11:09 ).
Meanwhile, the operator who cleared the high-speed Renfe Ave train to resume its journey before colliding with the stationary Iryo service has declined to be interviewed by the Civil Guard , according to Spanish media reports.
The revelation comes after several recordings from the incident were leaked to Spanish media , revealing parts of the critical communications in the final minutes before the crash and apparent confusion about the operation of the systems.
Separately, the train drivers’ union cautioned against drawing early conclusions about the incident, insisting on an extensive investigation into possible systemic failures that led to the tragedy.
We are also expecting to hear from Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente in the next 10-20 minutes.
I will bring you the key lines here.
Sources at Spain’s foreign ministry have confirmed that at least 51 foreign nationals from 23 different countries were involved in the crash.
Of those, two are believed to have died, nine were injured, and 18 are largely unharmed; the status of 22 remains unclear.
These numbers are likely to change as the identification process continues.
Portuguese authorities have confirmed that one crew member killed in the accident was Portuguese, according to El País and EFE.
Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez and Castilla–La Mancha president Emiliano García-Page have just briefed the media on the latest on the train crash on Wednesday.
